newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mrs Clinton sees Zimbabwe efforts to help people.
newsitem.headline: Mrs Clinton sees Zimbabwe efforts to help people.

text.p: U.S. first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on Saturday toured Zimbabwean programmes designed to help the disadvantaged and urged American investment in Africa to promote similar successes elsewhere.
"I'm hoping that Americans will understand how important it is that we support our friends in Africa," she told reporters.

"We have a lot at stake in making sure that countries like Zimbabwe are as successful as they can be and that they're able to deal with their problems in an effective manner," said President Clinton's wife, now halfway through a two-week tour of six African nations.
In a centre for the blind run by nuns in Harare, Mrs Clinton watched blind Zimbabwean children learn how to read braille.

At a family planning clinic, teenagers acted out a skit on a fairly common practice in Zimbabwe -- young women who deliver their newborn babies in secret and leave them for dead because they cannot afford to care for them.

And in a rustic church surrounded by cornfields, Mrs Clinton heard appeals from poor but energetic women to send sewing machines to help them get ahead. "I've looked everywhere, but there's no one like Jesus," they sang as Mrs. Clinton left.

Mrs Clinton, who is travelling with her daughter Chelsea, told reporters she believed her goodwill tour was helping generate new interest in America about Africa and urged U.S. companies to take advantage of a trend toward democracy and increase investment in the sub-Sahara.
At the Dorothy Duncan Centre for the Blind, Mrs. Clinton listened as Judith Makudzani, a 14-year-old blind student, read a poem by tracing her fingers across the lines of braille in her book.
"You'd make a very good lawyer," Mrs. Clinton, her voice gravally from a head cold, told Judith. "You have a very good voice."

At the Kuwadzana Health Clinic, Mrs. Clinton watched five Zimbabwean teenagers play out a scenario in the Shona tribal language in which one of them is pregnant and wants to keep the child, but the father will not marry her and her friends encourage her to dump it.
Mrs. Clinton also got a first-hand look at her own work toward persuading the U.S. Congress to approve $123 million in family planning money for needy nations.

Conservative Republicans in Congress had tried to block the money from being spent, saying it was going to encourage abortion practices. But President Clinton led the fight for the money and it was approved earlier this year.

A clinic official, Annah-Maria Mangwiro, explained how the clinic, funded in part by U.S. aid, encouraged use of various contraceptives to try to control Zimbabwe's population of 10.5 million, now growing at three percent a year. Abortion is illegal in the country.
Mangwiro said the birth rate was down from six children per mother in 1984 to 4.3 children per mother.

At Faith Church, about 50 women gathered inside and told how they were succeeding another project promoted by Mrs. Clinton, micro-credit, in which small amounts of money are loaned mostly to women to help them develop small businesses.
They expressed satisfaction at the help they were receiving but appealed to Mrs. Clinton to send sewing machines, knitting machines and other such items.
She said the United States had committed another $500,000 for their programme, the Zambuko Trust -- and pledged to see what she could do about the sewing machines.

Mrs. Clinton was to leave Harare on Sunday to tour the Victoria Falls, among other things. In the past week she has also visted Senegal and South Africa. She will stop in Tanzania, Uganda and Eritrea before returning to the United States on March 30.
